title: Attention Is All You Need
tldr: A translation network built only from attention trains far faster than recurrent models and sets new translation records.
newcomer: This paper sits in deep learning for language. To follow it you need how neural networks are built and trained, how earlier models read sentences one word at a time, and what 'attention' meant before this paper made it the whole model.

sections.name: Basics used throughout
sections.summary: The mathematics and computing every deep-learning paper takes for granted: vectors, probabilities, neural networks and how cost scales.
sections.role: Needed to read the equations, Table 1's complexity comparison and the training-cost numbers.

sections.name: Neural network building blocks
sections.summary: The standard layers and training tricks that deep networks are assembled from.
sections.role: The Transformer combines these familiar parts (embeddings, feed-forward layers, residuals, layer norm, dropout, Adam) around its new attention layers.

sections.name: Sequence models
sections.summary: How networks read and write sequences: recurrence, LSTMs, encoder–decoders and convolutional alternatives.
sections.role: The approaches the Transformer replaces, and the reason it can be trained in parallel.

sections.name: Translation and evaluation
sections.summary: The task, data, tokenisation, decoding and scoring used to judge translation models.
sections.role: How the results are measured: WMT 2014, byte-pair tokens, beam search, BLEU, and Penn Treebank parsing.

sections.name: Attention
sections.summary: Letting each word take a weighted look at other words, in place of reading them in order.
sections.role: The heart of the paper: scaled dot-product, multi-head self-attention and positional encodings.

concepts.name: Vectors and matrices
concepts.plain: Words become lists of numbers (vectors); a layer of a network multiplies them by a matrix of learned weights.
concepts.why_here: Every operation in the Transformer is a matrix multiplication, which is why it runs fast on GPUs.

concepts.name: Probability and softmax
concepts.plain: Softmax turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to one; training maximises the probability of the right next word.
concepts.why_here: Attention weights are a softmax over scores, and the output layer is a softmax over the vocabulary.

concepts.name: Neural networks and backpropagation
concepts.plain: Layers of simple units with adjustable weights, trained by nudging every weight downhill on the error (gradient descent), with gradients computed by backpropagation.
concepts.why_here: The Transformer is a neural network; the vanishing-gradient and scaling arguments depend on how gradients flow.

concepts.name: Complexity and parallel computing
concepts.plain: Big-O notation says how cost grows with input size; GPUs do many identical operations at once, so work that doesn't depend on earlier steps runs much faster.
concepts.why_here: The paper's argument is about sequential steps, path length and O(n²·d) cost, and its training cost is in GPU-days and FLOPs.

concepts.name: Word embeddings
concepts.plain: Each word (or word piece) is mapped to a learned vector, so similar words end up close together.
concepts.why_here: Input and output tokens are embedded into 512-dimensional vectors, sharing weights with the output layer.

concepts.name: Feed-forward layers and ReLU
concepts.plain: A fully connected layer applies a matrix and a simple non-linearity; ReLU keeps positive values and zeroes negatives.
concepts.why_here: Each Transformer layer has a position-wise feed-forward network with a ReLU in between.

concepts.name: Residual connections
concepts.plain: Adding a layer's input to its output (x + f(x)) lets signals and gradients skip past layers, making very deep networks trainable.
concepts.why_here: Every sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection.

concepts.name: Layer normalisation
concepts.plain: Rescales each vector to zero mean and unit variance before passing it on, which keeps training stable.
concepts.why_here: Applied after every residual connection: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)).

concepts.name: Dropout and label smoothing
concepts.plain: Ways to stop a network memorising its training data: randomly switching off units (dropout), or softening the target probabilities (label smoothing).
concepts.why_here: Both are used in training; the ablations show dropout matters.

concepts.name: Adam and learning-rate schedules
concepts.plain: Adam adapts each weight's step size from running averages of its gradients; a schedule warms the learning rate up and then decays it.
concepts.why_here: Training uses Adam with a 4000-step warm-up and inverse-square-root decay.

concepts.name: Convolutional networks
concepts.plain: Layers that slide the same small filter along the input, so each output sees only a local window.
concepts.why_here: Convolutional translation models are one of the two alternatives the paper compares against.

concepts.name: Language modelling and autoregression
concepts.plain: Predicting the next word from the words so far; generating text by repeatedly feeding each prediction back in (autoregression).
concepts.why_here: The decoder is autoregressive, which is why its self-attention must be masked.

concepts.name: Recurrent neural networks
concepts.plain: Networks that read a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward, so step t can't start before step t−1 finishes.
concepts.why_here: The model the Transformer replaces; its sequential nature is the problem being solved.

concepts.name: LSTMs and long-range dependencies
concepts.plain: Gated recurrent units that keep information over longer spans; even so, signals between distant words must pass through many steps, and gradients fade along the way.
concepts.why_here: The path-length argument for self-attention is about exactly this difficulty.

concepts.name: Encoder–decoder (seq2seq)
concepts.plain: One network encodes the input sentence into vectors; another decodes them into the output sentence, word by word.
concepts.why_here: The Transformer keeps this structure, building both halves from attention.

concepts.name: Convolutional sequence models
concepts.plain: Translation models built from convolutions (ByteNet, ConvS2S) that process all positions in parallel, but need several layers to connect distant words.
concepts.why_here: The paper's closest competitors; ConvS2S also supplies the learned positional embeddings it compares with.

concepts.name: Machine translation and WMT
concepts.plain: Automatically translating text between languages; WMT is the yearly shared benchmark with standard training and test sets.
concepts.why_here: The main task: WMT 2014 English→German and English→French.

concepts.name: Subword tokens (byte-pair encoding)
concepts.plain: Splitting words into frequent pieces so rare words can still be represented with a fixed vocabulary.
concepts.why_here: Sentences are encoded with a 37k byte-pair vocabulary (German) or 32k word pieces (French).

concepts.name: Beam search
concepts.plain: Instead of always taking the single most likely next word, keep the few best partial translations at each step.
concepts.why_here: Used at test time with beam size 4 and a length penalty.

concepts.name: BLEU score
concepts.plain: An automatic translation score (0–100) based on how many word sequences overlap with human reference translations.
concepts.why_here: All translation results are reported in BLEU.

concepts.name: Constituency parsing
concepts.plain: Recovering the phrase structure of a sentence as a tree; the Penn Treebank's Wall Street Journal section is the standard test, scored by F1.
concepts.why_here: The test of whether the Transformer works beyond translation.

concepts.name: Queries, keys and values
concepts.plain: A soft lookup: a query is compared with every key, the scores become weights, and the output is the weighted average of the values.
concepts.why_here: The paper defines all its attention in these terms.

concepts.name: Masked decoder attention
concepts.plain: Hiding future positions (setting their scores to −∞) so each word can only attend to the words before it.
concepts.why_here: Keeps the decoder autoregressive while training on whole sentences at once.

concepts.name: Attention in translation
concepts.plain: Letting the decoder take a weighted look at all source words at each step, rather than squeezing the sentence into one vector.
concepts.why_here: The ingredient the paper keeps while throwing away recurrence.

concepts.name: Self-attention
concepts.plain: Attention within a single sequence: every word builds its new representation by attending to every other word of the same sentence.
concepts.why_here: The core of both encoder and decoder, connecting any two words in a single step.

concepts.name: Scaled dot-product attention
concepts.plain: Scores are dot products of queries and keys divided by √d_k, so they don't grow with dimension and push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients.
concepts.why_here: The paper's attention function; the scaling is its fix for large key sizes.

concepts.name: Multi-head attention
concepts.plain: Running several attention operations in parallel on different learned projections, so different heads can track different relationships.
concepts.why_here: Uses 8 heads; ablations show 1 head is 0.9 BLEU worse.

concepts.name: Positional encoding
concepts.plain: Attention ignores order, so a signal giving each position's place in the sentence is added to its embedding: here, sine and cosine waves of different wavelengths.
concepts.why_here: The paper's way of giving the model word order without recurrence.
